newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS - Prices end down 1/4 to 3/8.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS - Prices end down 1/4 to 3/8.

text.p: U.S. municipal bond prices ended down 1/4 to 3/8 of a point or more in spots as customers continued to sit on their hands.
"There doesn't seem to be a customer base that's compelled or wants to buy bonds in any way, shape or form," one trader said.

Monday's uneventful session continued the "downward spiral that we seem to have been in for the last couple of weeks," he said. And, with few new issues to focus on, the market appears to be in for "a drag of a week," the trader said.
A municipal analyst also described the market as quiet, judging it down 1/4 to 3/8 of a point to more in spots. Most activity was on quotes, he said.
High-grade issues weakened by two to three basis points, with softness most evident on the long end, the analyst said. Dollar bonds closed down 3/8 of a point, he said.

Monday's active issues included Delaware River Port Authority of Pennsylvania and New Jersey 5-1/2 percent bonds of 2026. The bonds bid a 5.82 percent net yield and were offered at a 5.77 percent net Monday. The bonds closed Thursday's session with no bid, but were offered at a 5.76 percent net yield.

In the government market, the benchmark 30-year bond closed down 5/32 at 94-4/32 to yield 7.10 percent. In debt futures, the June municipal contract closed down 8/32 at 111-20/32. The June T-bond contract closed down 5/32 at 107-7/32. The MOB spread was 141 ticks.

Monday's economic news included the U.S. Commerce Department's report that February personal income rose 0.9 percent, while spending increased 0.3 percent. The income increase was the largest since June 1996.

Also Monday, the March Chicago Purchasing Management index rose to 57.5 from 56.2 in February. Forecasts had been for 57.0. Prices paid was reported at 57.4 from 56.0 and employment at 53.4 from 49.9.

Tuesday's economic news includes the National Association of Purchasing Management's March survey at 1000 EST. Economists polled by Reuters expect a reading of 53.6 percent, up from 53.1 percent in February.

Looking ahead to Tuesday's new issues, seven negotiated offerings are scheduled totaling $223 million. The largest is an $88 million Harris County Industrial Development Corporation, Texas, variable rate deal via Bear Stearns & Co. Another 11 deals totaling $193 million are possible.
On the competitive side, 16 sales are scheduled totaling $132 million. The largest is a $29 million Broome County, N.Y., offering set for 1100 EST.
For the week, scheduled negotiated and competitive issues combined are expected to number 68 and total $1.347 billion.
A $176 million King County, Wash., stadium offering via Smith Barney Inc tops the negotiated list, while Broome County's offering is expected to be the largest competitive deal.
